Lochner v. New York. In 1905, the Supreme Court struck down a state labor law as a violation of the Due Process Clause, initiating an era in which the Court systematically invalidated economic and labor regulations.

In 1897, New York enacted a Maximum Hours Law restricting bakers to ten hours per day and sixty hours per week, citing health and safety. Long hours weakened workers' health, and the flour dust and heat of bakeries posed particular risks. Joseph Lochner, a bakery owner, required employees to work longer hours anyway and was fined fifty dollars. He appealed, arguing the law violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, which protects liberty and property, including the liberty to negotiate with employees.

Justice Peckham wrote for a five-to-four majority. He held that the Due Process Clause protects substantive rights, not merely procedural regularity. The general right to make a contract in relation to one's business is part of the liberty protected by the Due Process Clause. Freedom of contract is a natural and fundamental liberty that the state cannot restrict except to protect legitimate police power—health, safety, morals. The majority characterized the bakers' law as a labor regulation disguised as health protection, really just redistributing bargaining power. They found no legitimate state interest justifying it.

Justice Holmes's dissent is more cited today than Peckham's majority. Holmes wrote that the Fourteenth Amendment does not enact Mr. Herbert Spencer's Social Statics—that is, the Constitution does not embed laissez-faire economics into law. If the legislature rationally believed the law protected health, courts should defer to democratic judgment. Justice Harlan's longer dissent outlined the evidence of bakers' poor health and the legitimacy of the regulation.

The Lochner era lasted from 1905 to 1937. The Court struck down approximately two hundred state and federal laws—minimum wage laws, price controls, union regulations, workplace safety rules—as violations of freedom of contract. Adair v. United States invalidated a federal law prohibiting employers from firing workers for union membership. Coppage v. Kansas struck down a state law banning yellow-dog contracts, agreements not to join unions. The Court's stance frustrated reformers and impeded the Progressive movement and New Deal legislation.

Then came the reversal. During the New Deal, as FDR proposed court-packing, Justice Owen Roberts switched sides in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish in 1937, upholding a minimum wage law. The Court abandoned Lochner. Congress and the states now had broad power to regulate economic life under the commerce power, and due process became a weak constraint.

Lochner is dead as precedent but it haunts debates over unenumerated rights. Does the Due Process Clause protect privacy? Gun ownership? All rest on Lochner-like reasoning—finding rights not in the text. Modern conservatives occasionally invoke Lochner-like arguments against regulations, though they disclaim the label. Progressives invoke Lochner as a cautionary tale about judicial overreach. The case remains unresolved in constitutional philosophy, even as its specific holdings are repudiated.
